I've been a nurse for 24 years, and for 11 of them my entire job was other people's bowels.

Then I went on Mounjaro, and it happened to me. My own bathroom cabinet had six things in it and not one worked for more than a week.

Not until May, when a doctor said one sentence to me that I should have been told in January.

By then it had already cost me the worst night of 24 years on that floor.

I haven't repeated any of this to a single person I work with. I'm about to put all of it on the internet with my name on it.

My name is Hannah. I'm 56 and I've been on the same med-surg floor since I was 32.

For 11 of those years I did the prep teaching for our GI lab. I'm the one who hands you the jug and tells you, kindly, that yes, you do have to drink all of it.

I added it up on a quiet night shift once, for no reason except that I was curious. 430 people I've handed that sheet to. Water. Fiber. Keep moving.

I believed every word of it. It's good advice.

It's the right advice for ordinary people. I didn't find out there's a group of us it's wrong for until I became one of them.

And when it goes bad on that floor, I'm the one they call. Everybody there knows it.

There's a rule about this in my profession. If something is going on with you that affects your ability to do your job, you report it. You don't sit at home and decide on your own that you're fine.

I didn't report it. And I'll tell you the honest reason, which isn't the one you'd guess. It wasn't the shame, although there was plenty of that.

It was that I knew the second I said it out loud, somebody was going to take my prescription away.

So. The medication.

I started last October, and I need to be clear about this next part.

The shot worked. 61 pounds. My A1c is the best it's been since I was 40. My knees stopped hurting on a 12 hour shift, which I'd quietly accepted was just what the rest of my life was going to feel like.

And the food noise stopped. I've never been able to explain that one to anybody who hasn't had it. It was there every waking minute since I was 15, and then it was gone.

I wasn't giving that up. Not for anything.

That's the whole reason this got as bad as it did.

I didn't know it that October, but I was already about six months out from the worst night of my career.

There's no day one with this. It comes on so slow that you never get a morning where you decide something is wrong.

By December I was sick most of the day.

I assumed that was the medication. Everybody assumes that's the medication. It's the famous one, it's on the label, and it's what my own doctor said when I brought it up.

I was wrong about that, and it took me until May to find out why. Hold onto it, because it's the part I most want somebody to read.

I also stopped going.

I'd gone every single morning of my adult life. Six ten in the morning, before work, 30 years, and I never once thought about it, which is the thing about a body that works. You don't notice it.

By December it was every second day. By January it was every fourth or fifth. Then I stopped being able to predict it at all, and I started keeping a number in my head. What day I was on. I didn't decide to do that. It was just always there, the way you always roughly know what time it is.

So in January I did the sensible thing. I want you to notice that I did the sensible thing, because of what it got me.

I told my doctor. I said it had been 6 days and that I was worried about it.

He didn't look up from the screen.

He said, "Are you drinking enough water? Try to get a little more fiber in there."

Then he said, "Now. Your A1c. This is wonderful."

That was the appointment.

I have an opinion about it. I've had 8 months to sit with it and I'm going to keep it professional. But I have one.

So I did what everybody does. I started buying.

Metamucil first, because that's what I'd just been told to do. When that did nothing I went to psyllium on its own. When that did nothing either I started on Miralax, a capful in my coffee every morning, because that's the only way I would get it down.

The Miralax worked for about 10 days. So I added magnesium at night. That worked for about a week. So I doubled it.

Then stool softeners, two with breakfast, on top of all of it.

Then prunes. Prune juice. Warm prune juice with butter melted into it, which is exactly as bad as it sounds.

And then the thing nobody wants to admit they've bought. Enemas, in a paper bag, from a pharmacy two towns over, because I didn't want to be seen buying them at the one by our house.

By March I was taking five things every single day just to stay level, with an extra dose on Sunday nights before my shot because Mondays were always the worst.

I was still going about once a week.

Every one of those things worked for a few days. Not one of them worked for a month.

And here's the part I've never said to anybody, because I know some of you are sitting in it right now.

I was doing the math. 61 pounds and the best bloodwork of my adult life, against not being able to go to the bathroom.

My husband asked me once, in March, standing at the sink.

Ray is a retired firefighter. 29 years married, and there's very little he hasn't seen or heard.

He said, "Are you okay? Because you are not okay."

I told him I was tired. I looked straight at him and lied about it, and he let it go because I asked him to.

Now April.

I had a patient in 412 who had come in at the start of the month. 80 years old. I'm changing his name, so let's call him Denny.

He called me boss. Every single time. "Morning, boss." He asked about my grandson by name and he got the name right, which almost nobody does, because it isn't a name people expect.

He was doing well. He was going home that week.

The night it happened I was on day 8 myself.

I want to be honest about what 8 days does, because I don't think people understand that it stops being about the bathroom. You're frightened. And I know what a bowel looks like when it's been left too long, because I've stood there and looked at the films. Knowing more didn't help me. It made it worse.

I went into the bathroom on four, past the chapel, at about two thirty, because it's the one nobody uses.

I was in there long enough that I'd stopped trying. I was sitting with my head against the wall, sweating, trying to figure out whether I was going to have to go somewhere myself and be the patient.

And then I heard it. You know the sound before you know what it is. The overhead, and then the running.

412.

I got up and my legs went and I sat back down.

I've gone over this more times than is good for me. It wasn't that I decided to stay. It was that I couldn't straighten up, and I couldn't get my clothes right, and I was shaking too bad to do either.

Tanya knocked on the door twice.

I didn't answer her.

By the time I got out there it was finished. They had him back. He was fine, or as fine as an 80 year old man is after that.

Four minutes. That's my own estimate. I've never checked it against the record because I don't want to know.

The next morning he called me boss.

And nobody said one word to me about that door. Not Tanya. Not anybody.

That's the part I didn't expect and haven't been able to put down since. There was no consequence. Nobody even asked. I got away with it completely, and I've found that far harder to live with than being caught.

I sat in my car in the staff lot before I drove home, and I cried for about 20 minutes. I haven't cried like that since my mother.

In May there was blood.

I can talk myself out of most things. I couldn't talk myself out of that.

So I let one of our GI docs get me on his schedule, and he scoped me in the middle of the month.

It came back clear. Nothing sinister.

Afterwards he sat down on the end of the gurney while I was still coming out of it, and he asked me what I'd been taking for it.

I listed it. All of it. It took a while.

He said, "None of that was ever going to work. Every one of those treats what's already in the pipe. Nobody's looking at the pipe."

I asked him what he meant.

"Bile. You only make it when there's food to break down. You're barely eating. So you're barely making any."

I said I still didn't see what that had to do with it.

"Because breaking food down isn't the only thing it does. It's what keeps the colon slick enough for anything to move through it. No bile, nothing's slick. It dries out and it stops."

Then I asked him about the sickness. The thing I'd been blaming on the shot since December.

He said, "That's not the drug. That's you being full. It's got nowhere to go but back up."

And then the sentence. The one I said at the top of this.

"And you've all been putting fiber on top of it. Which is like unblocking a toilet by pushing more paper down it."

Then he shrugged and went off to write it up, because to him this wasn't a revelation. It was a Tuesday.

I went home and sat on the edge of the bed with my coat still on.

Because it explained all of it. The prunes. The gallon of water I was tracking in an app. The paper bag from a pharmacy in another town. Five months of it, all aimed at the wrong end.

It also meant there was nothing in my bathroom cabinet that was ever going to help me. Every single one of those things is built to push from the bottom.

And then I worked out the second half of it, sitting there, and that was worse.

Because I did nothing about it for three weeks.

I want to be honest about that as well, because it's the strangest part of the whole thing. I knew exactly what was wrong with me. A man had just drawn me the diagram. And I still went to the pharmacy that Saturday and bought more Miralax, because it was the only thing on the shelf and I didn't know what else a person was supposed to do.

I got quietly worse.

Then Tanya.

First week of June, in the locker room, nobody else in there.

She said, "I knocked on that door in April."

I didn't say anything.

She said, "I knew what you were doing in there. Because it's what I do in there."

Tanya's been on Wegovy since last spring. We work three shifts a week together, and neither of us had said one word to the other one.

She had a bottle in her lunch bag. She said she'd been carrying it around for a week trying to figure out how to bring any of this up with me.

I'm the last woman alive who buys a supplement. I've spent 24 years watching people arrive on my floor with shopping bags full of bottles they saw on Facebook, and what's being sold to women on this medication right now is the worst of it. Half of it is the same fiber blend that was a prebiotic three years ago with GLP-1 printed on the front in a new font.

She said, "I know. Read the back of it before you tell me I've lost my mind."

So I stood there in my coat and read the back of it.

Omyo. I'd never heard of it. That didn't help.

14 things. Not one I had to look up, and not one I'd have flagged for a patient.

The first three were milk thistle, dandelion and beetroot.

Those are bile. All three of them.

That's the only reason I didn't hand it straight back to her. Not because I believed it. Because it was the only thing anybody had put in front of me that was aimed at the right end.

Then ginger and artichoke, which are for the squeeze. Your gut moves everything along by squeezing, and on this medication that slows way down with the rest of you. Slick on its own isn't enough. Something still has to push.

And nothing that forces anything. No senna. Nothing in there that was going to want a bigger dose out of me next month, which after five months of doubling everything was the part I stood there and read twice.

I still thought it was probably nothing. I'd spent about $400 that year on things that worked for a week, and I'd run out of ways to be hopeful about any of it.

But it was the only thing anybody had handed me that started at the top.

Two capsules before bed. I started it on a Tuesday.

I want to be honest about the first two days, because if you're the kind of person who gives something 48 hours before you decide it's another waste of money, you'd have thrown it out.

Nothing Tuesday. Nothing Wednesday.

Thursday morning I went, and it wasn't dramatic. It was just easy. No bracing myself, nothing taken alongside it, no 20 minutes.

I was still skeptical. It was one time.

Omyo.

Twenty-one botanicals. No psyllium, no senna, nothing that swells and nothing you build a tolerance to."

"I have women in this practice who have been on it a year. It's the reason most of them are still on their medication."

"Made in the USA in an FDA-registered facility. Money-back guarantee. If it doesn't work for you, send it back."

I've been a nurse for 24 years, and for 11 of them my entire job was other people's bowels.

Then I went on Mounjaro, and it happened to me. My own bathroom cabinet had six things in it and not one worked for more than a week.

Not until May, when a doctor said one sentence to me that I should have been told in January.

By then it had already cost me the worst night of 24 years on that floor.

I haven't repeated any of this to a single person I work with. I'm about to put all of it on the internet with my name on it.

My name is Hannah. I'm 56 and I've been on the same med-surg floor since I was 32.

For 11 of those years I did the prep teaching for our GI lab. I'm the one who hands you the jug and tells you, kindly, that yes, you do have to drink all of it.

I added it up on a quiet night shift once, for no reason except that I was curious. 430 people I've handed that sheet to. Water. Fiber. Keep moving.

I believed every word of it. It's good advice.

It's the right advice for ordinary people. I didn't find out there's a group of us it's wrong for until I became one of them.

And when it goes bad on that floor, I'm the one they call. Everybody there knows it.

There's a rule about this in my profession. If something is going on with you that affects your ability to do your job, you report it. You don't sit at home and decide on your own that you're fine.

I didn't report it. And I'll tell you the honest reason, which isn't the one you'd guess. It wasn't the shame, although there was plenty of that.

It was that I knew the second I said it out loud, somebody was going to take my prescription away.

So. The medication.

I started last October, and I need to be clear about this next part.

The shot worked. 61 pounds. My A1c is the best it's been since I was 40. My knees stopped hurting on a 12 hour shift, which I'd quietly accepted was just what the rest of my life was going to feel like.

And the food noise stopped. I've never been able to explain that one to anybody who hasn't had it. It was there every waking minute since I was 15, and then it was gone.

I wasn't giving that up. Not for anything.

That's the whole reason this got as bad as it did.

I didn't know it that October, but I was already about six months out from the worst night of my career.

There's no day one with this. It comes on so slow that you never get a morning where you decide something is wrong.

By December I was sick most of the day.

I assumed that was the medication. Everybody assumes that's the medication. It's the famous one, it's on the label, and it's what my own doctor said when I brought it up.

I was wrong about that, and it took me until May to find out why. Hold onto it, because it's the part I most want somebody to read.

I also stopped going.

I'd gone every single morning of my adult life. Six ten in the morning, before work, 30 years, and I never once thought about it, which is the thing about a body that works. You don't notice it.

By December it was every second day. By January it was every fourth or fifth. Then I stopped being able to predict it at all, and I started keeping a number in my head. What day I was on. I didn't decide to do that. It was just always there, the way you always roughly know what time it is.

So in January I did the sensible thing. I want you to notice that I did the sensible thing, because of what it got me.

I told my doctor. I said it had been 6 days and that I was worried about it.

He didn't look up from the screen.

He said, "Are you drinking enough water? Try to get a little more fiber in there."

Then he said, "Now. Your A1c. This is wonderful."

That was the appointment.

I have an opinion about it. I've had 8 months to sit with it and I'm going to keep it professional. But I have one.

So I did what everybody does. I started buying.

Metamucil first, because that's what I'd just been told to do. When that did nothing I went to psyllium on its own. When that did nothing either I started on Miralax, a capful in my coffee every morning, because that's the only way I would get it down.

The Miralax worked for about 10 days. So I added magnesium at night. That worked for about a week. So I doubled it.

Then stool softeners, two with breakfast, on top of all of it.

Then prunes. Prune juice. Warm prune juice with butter melted into it, which is exactly as bad as it sounds.

And then the thing nobody wants to admit they've bought. Enemas, in a paper bag, from a pharmacy two towns over, because I didn't want to be seen buying them at the one by our house.

By March I was taking five things every single day just to stay level, with an extra dose on Sunday nights before my shot because Mondays were always the worst.

I was still going about once a week.

Every one of those things worked for a few days. Not one of them worked for a month.

And here's the part I've never said to anybody, because I know some of you are sitting in it right now.

I was doing the math. 61 pounds and the best bloodwork of my adult life, against not being able to go to the bathroom.

My husband asked me once, in March, standing at the sink.

Ray is a retired firefighter. 29 years married, and there's very little he hasn't seen or heard.

He said, "Are you okay? Because you are not okay."

I told him I was tired. I looked straight at him and lied about it, and he let it go because I asked him to.

Now April.

I had a patient in 412 who had come in at the start of the month. 80 years old. I'm changing his name, so let's call him Denny.

He called me boss. Every single time. "Morning, boss." He asked about my grandson by name and he got the name right, which almost nobody does, because it isn't a name people expect.

He was doing well. He was going home that week.

The night it happened I was on day 8 myself.

I want to be honest about what 8 days does, because I don't think people understand that it stops being about the bathroom. You're frightened. And I know what a bowel looks like when it's been left too long, because I've stood there and looked at the films. Knowing more didn't help me. It made it worse.

I went into the bathroom on four, past the chapel, at about two thirty, because it's the one nobody uses.

I was in there long enough that I'd stopped trying. I was sitting with my head against the wall, sweating, trying to figure out whether I was going to have to go somewhere myself and be the patient.

And then I heard it. You know the sound before you know what it is. The overhead, and then the running.

412.

I got up and my legs went and I sat back down.

I've gone over this more times than is good for me. It wasn't that I decided to stay. It was that I couldn't straighten up, and I couldn't get my clothes right, and I was shaking too bad to do either.

Tanya knocked on the door twice.

I didn't answer her.

By the time I got out there it was finished. They had him back. He was fine, or as fine as an 80 year old man is after that.

Four minutes. That's my own estimate. I've never checked it against the record because I don't want to know.

The next morning he called me boss.

And nobody said one word to me about that door. Not Tanya. Not anybody.

That's the part I didn't expect and haven't been able to put down since. There was no consequence. Nobody even asked. I got away with it completely, and I've found that far harder to live with than being caught.

I sat in my car in the staff lot before I drove home, and I cried for about 20 minutes. I haven't cried like that since my mother.

In May there was blood.

I can talk myself out of most things. I couldn't talk myself out of that.

So I let one of our GI docs get me on his schedule, and he scoped me in the middle of the month.

It came back clear. Nothing sinister.

Afterwards he sat down on the end of the gurney while I was still coming out of it, and he asked me what I'd been taking for it.

I listed it. All of it. It took a while.

He said, "None of that was ever going to work. Every one of those treats what's already in the pipe. Nobody's looking at the pipe."

I asked him what he meant.

"Bile. You only make it when there's food to break down. You're barely eating. So you're barely making any."

I said I still didn't see what that had to do with it.

"Because breaking food down isn't the only thing it does. It's what keeps the colon slick enough for anything to move through it. No bile, nothing's slick. It dries out and it stops."

Then I asked him about the sickness. The thing I'd been blaming on the shot since December.

He said, "That's not the drug. That's you being full. It's got nowhere to go but back up."

And then the sentence. The one I said at the top of this.

"And you've all been putting fiber on top of it. Which is like unblocking a toilet by pushing more paper down it."

Then he shrugged and went off to write it up, because to him this wasn't a revelation. It was a Tuesday.

I went home and sat on the edge of the bed with my coat still on.

Because it explained all of it. The prunes. The gallon of water I was tracking in an app. The paper bag from a pharmacy in another town. Five months of it, all aimed at the wrong end.

It also meant there was nothing in my bathroom cabinet that was ever going to help me. Every single one of those things is built to push from the bottom.

And then I worked out the second half of it, sitting there, and that was worse.

Because I did nothing about it for three weeks.

I want to be honest about that as well, because it's the strangest part of the whole thing. I knew exactly what was wrong with me. A man had just drawn me the diagram. And I still went to the pharmacy that Saturday and bought more Miralax, because it was the only thing on the shelf and I didn't know what else a person was supposed to do.

I got quietly worse.

Then Tanya.

First week of June, in the locker room, nobody else in there.

She said, "I knocked on that door in April."

I didn't say anything.

She said, "I knew what you were doing in there. Because it's what I do in there."

Tanya's been on Wegovy since last spring. We work three shifts a week together, and neither of us had said one word to the other one.

She had a bottle in her lunch bag. She said she'd been carrying it around for a week trying to figure out how to bring any of this up with me.

I'm the last woman alive who buys a supplement. I've spent 24 years watching people arrive on my floor with shopping bags full of bottles they saw on Facebook, and what's being sold to women on this medication right now is the worst of it. Half of it is the same fiber blend that was a prebiotic three years ago with GLP-1 printed on the front in a new font.

She said, "I know. Read the back of it before you tell me I've lost my mind."

So I stood there in my coat and read the back of it.

Omyo. I'd never heard of it. That didn't help.

14 things. Not one I had to look up, and not one I'd have flagged for a patient.

The first three were milk thistle, dandelion and beetroot.

Those are bile. All three of them.

That's the only reason I didn't hand it straight back to her. Not because I believed it. Because it was the only thing anybody had put in front of me that was aimed at the right end.

Then ginger and artichoke, which are for the squeeze. Your gut moves everything along by squeezing, and on this medication that slows way down with the rest of you. Slick on its own isn't enough. Something still has to push.

And nothing that forces anything. No senna. Nothing in there that was going to want a bigger dose out of me next month, which after five months of doubling everything was the part I stood there and read twice.

I still thought it was probably nothing. I'd spent about $400 that year on things that worked for a week, and I'd run out of ways to be hopeful about any of it.

But it was the only thing anybody had handed me that started at the top.

Two capsules before bed. I started it on a Tuesday.

I want to be honest about the first two days, because if you're the kind of person who gives something 48 hours before you decide it's another waste of money, you'd have thrown it out.

Nothing Tuesday. Nothing Wednesday.

Thursday morning I went, and it wasn't dramatic. It was just easy. No bracing myself, nothing taken alongside it, no 20 minutes.

I was still skeptical. It was one time.

Week one I went three times. I'd been going about once a week, so that number meant something to me that it won't mean to anybody else.

Week two I noticed my waistband before I noticed anything else. And I could breathe lying down, which I hadn't been able to do since February and had somehow decided was just how I slept now.

Week three the sickness stopped. I'd decided that was the price of the medication and that I was stuck with it for as long as I stayed on.

Week five I realized I didn't know what day I was on.

I'd carried that number every waking minute for five months. I didn't decide to stop. I noticed one morning, brushing my teeth, that it wasn't there, and I can't tell you when it went.

In July we had another one. A woman on the other side of the floor.

I heard the overhead and I stood up and I went, and I was the first one through that door.

I hadn't been sure I could still do that. I'd been carrying it around since April, quietly, that maybe I wasn't that person anymore.

Tanya saw me go. She's never said anything about it and she never will, and that's fine, because we both know.

Then there's Charlene.

Charlene is one of ours. I told her about it at the end of June, once I was sure it wasn't a fluke, and she said she'd order some. She meant it at the time. You know how that goes.

She switched to a different shot instead, because somebody told her it was better on that one. It followed her straight over. Of course it did.

She came off the medication altogether in July. She'd lost 30 pounds and her blood pressure was normal for the first time in 9 years.

She's put 19 of it back on since.

She said to me two weeks ago, "I wish I'd just ordered it when you told me."

That's the one I think about. Not my own bad nights. The women who did everything right, finally got the thing they'd been chasing half their lives, and handed it back over something that had a fix nobody had bothered to tell them about.

And I know what people say about April. He lived, so no harm done.

I don't find that comforting and I'm not going to pretend I do.

So here's why I'm putting my name on this.

If you used to go every single morning without ever thinking about it, and then it was every second day, and then it was every fourth, and now you couldn't tell me when it was.

If you're sick most of the day and you've been blaming the shot for it.

If you're taking three or four things every night just to stay level, and every one of them worked for a week and then it didn't.

If you've started quietly asking yourself whether all of this is worth it.

And you don't have to be standing in a hospital for this to be taking something from you. Most of what it takes, it takes quietly.

What I wanted back wasn't complicated. I wanted to stop thinking about it all day. I wanted to trust my own body again and get on with things.

I haven't told my manager.

Denny went home four days after that night. He came past the desk on his way out and he told me I was the best one on that floor and he called me boss one more time.

I've never corrected him.

That's the woman I'd like to go on being, and for the first time since last winter I think I might be her again.

6 months on the shot. 36 pounds down. 6 days since I'd gone.

And at my daughter's wedding, an 86-year-old Greek woman I had never met asked me the one question nobody else had thought to ask.

I am Hannah. I am fifty-four. I have two daughters. In April the younger one, Kate, married a Greek boy named Nikos, down in Florida. I spent twenty-nine years in medical records at a hospital in central Ohio. Not a nurse. I filed charts, coded charts and read charts. That matters later, because it is the only reason I checked any of this.

I had never been to a Greek wedding. I packed a box of Miralax for it.

Here is what the six months actually looked like.

I started last October. By the wedding I was down thirty-six pounds and my blood pressure was 118 over 74, a number I had not seen on myself since I was thirty-five. The first two months I was happier than I had been in ten years. I would make the same decision again tomorrow.

Then somewhere in the second month, I stopped going.

Not slowed down. Stopped.

Three days. Then five. In January I went seven, and by the seventh day there was an ache low on the left side, and I spent an afternoon in the bathroom with the door locked, pressing on my own stomach and reading about what a blockage feels like.

The part I could not explain to my husband Ray was that I was not hungry at all and I was swollen all the time. I was eating maybe eight hundred calories a day and I looked six months pregnant by four in the afternoon.

Then the rest of it arrived. Tired in a way that walking did not fix. Not sleepy. Heavy. The scale sat at 189 for three weeks and I could not tell you whether the medicine had quit on me or whether I was carrying a week of it around. Ray asked if I was all right. I said I was fine.

I was not fine, and I could not have told him which part of it was making me not fine.

And I had a drawer.

If you have a drawer like this you already know where this is going.

Miralax. A tub of it, and a second one behind it. Metamucil, orange, half gone, because I could not get the last swallow down without gagging. Stool softeners, two brands. Fiber gummies. Prune juice. Chia seeds. A bag of ground flax that went rancid in the pantry.

And a note on my phone where I tracked the days.

I went to my doctor about it twice. Dr. Okafor is a good doctor and I want to be fair to her. Bloodwork normal. Nothing on the exam.

Both times she told me the same thing, honestly: "Hannah, this is the most common thing I deal with on these medications. You are eating a fraction of what you used to eat. Less going in means less coming out."

Hold on to that sentence. She was right, and it still cost me five more months.

Then she told me to drink more water. Eat more fiber. Walk. Keep the Miralax going.

I walked out of that office both times feeling believed and completely alone.

Because I was already drinking eighty ounces a day. I was already walking. And I was eating so little that "more fiber" did not connect to anything real. More fiber on top of what? I was not eating enough for fiber to hold on to.

So I did what I think most women do. I pushed harder. A stronger thing whenever the softer thing stopped working.

In February they moved me up a dose. Nobody told me what that would do to the other thing. And the number on my phone stopped coming back down.

Two weeks before the wedding, I sat in my car in a grocery store parking lot and did arithmetic.

I worked out how many pounds I would put back on if I stopped the shot. How long it would take. What I would say to Kate and to Ray.

I sat there for eleven minutes seriously considering giving back the best six months my body has had in twenty years, because I could not go to the bathroom.

I know I am not the only woman who has done that math in a parked car. I also know women who finished the math and stopped. Not one of them stopped because the shot was not working. They stopped because of this.

I did not stop. I went to the wedding — where a stranger asked me for the number I had never said out loud.

If you have never sat through a Greek reception, it is food, and it does not stop coming. Refusing it is not a diet choice in that room. It is close to an insult.

And I could not eat. I moved lamb around a plate for two hours with my hand flat on my stomach under the tablecloth, because the pressure was making it hard to sit up straight.

Nikos's grandmother was seated to my left. Her name was Eleni. Eighty-six, small, in black, white hair pinned back. She ate slowly and not much. She got up twice to cross the room, both times without pushing off the table.

About two hours in she turned to me and said: "Hannah. May I ask you something rude?"

I said of course.

She said: "You are not eating. And you are still full. How many days?"

I froze.

I had not told anybody that number. Not Ray. Not Kate. Not my sister. It was a note on my phone and I had never once said it out loud to another human being.

I said: "What do you mean?"

She said: "You have had your hand on your stomach since you sat down. You have moved the same piece of lamb four times. You have not eaten, and you are not hungry, and you are still swollen. I know that. How many days?"

I sat at my own daughter's wedding and said: "Six."

She nodded. She asked if I was eating so little because I was sick. I said no — I was on one of the shots, for the weight.

I said that part easily. Everybody knows somebody on one now. That was not the hard thing to say at that table. The hard thing to say was "six."

She said: "I do not know anything about your shot. But I know about not eating."

Then she turned back to her plate and finished eating.

Ray had asked me if I was all right. More than once. That was the question he had. He did not have the other one — and he had been looking at me every day for twenty-six years, which turns out to be the worst way to notice that something has changed.

Eleni had never seen me before in her life. She had two hours and clear eyes.

Ten minutes later she set her fork down and asked me to walk outside with her.

She took me out the side door to a concrete yard where they park the vans. There was a card table against the fence, in the shade, with newspaper on it, and on the newspaper were bunches of something long-stemmed and dark and wild-looking, half wilted from the sun.

"Do you know these?"

I said no.

"Horta. Wild greens. Dandelion. Chicory. Artichoke. We boil them with lemon. They are bitter. Americans do not like them."

She picked up a stem and held it out to me. Then she asked: "Do you know that we fast?"

I said I knew a little. Lent, I assumed.

"Not only Lent. Wednesday. Friday. Forty days before Easter. Forty before Christmas. Half of every year for eighty years I have eaten almost nothing. My mother the same. Her mother the same. We have known for a very long time what happens to a woman's body when the food stops."

I asked what happens.

"Everything stops. Not just the eating. Everything."

And then she said the thing I have thought about nearly every day since.

"You keep trying to push. Nobody has asked you what stopped."

I did not have an answer.

She meant that literally. I did not hear it that way for another month.

She sat down on a folding chair and told me about her husband. Kostas died in 2011, and she stopped eating — not on purpose, the way people stop eating when the person they cooked for is gone. Coffee and bread for most of a year.

By spring she had exactly what I had. Nothing moving. Swollen all the time. Not hungry at all.

Her own doctor told her to drink more water.

Her aunt, ninety-one, drove over, looked in her kitchen, and told her what the old women there all know.

Eleni told it to me standing in that lot in her black dress with a bunch of dandelion greens in her hand.

"When you eat, your liver sends down the bitter water. That is what takes your food apart. That is what makes everything slide."

"When you stop eating, the liver goes to sleep. Nothing comes down. So the food sits. It goes heavy. It goes sour. And nothing moves."

"You are not blocked. You are dry."

I asked what you do about it.

"You eat something bitter. The gut tells the liver. The liver does not know whether food is coming. It only knows bitter. That is why we eat these. Not because it is healthy. Because it is bitter."

I asked what happened to her after she started again. She said seven weeks, maybe eight. And then she stopped counting the days, and has not worried about it since.

I spent twenty-nine years reading charts. I am not a person who takes medical advice from a folding chair in a parking lot.

But I could not stop thinking about the fact that an eighty-six-year-old woman had watched me for two hours and known the number.

I asked her whether she really expected me to start boiling weeds. She laughed at me — the first time she laughed all night — and said: "They probably sell the bitter part in a bottle now. Ask at a pharmacy."

Then she took a place card off the nearest table, turned it over, and wrote three words on the back in shaky capitals.

Dandelion. Chicory. Artichoke.

She handed it to me and said: "These three. This is what your body is asking for. Ask your doctor before you take anything. If she says no, do not take it. But ask her."

I put the place card in my purse and went back inside and danced with my daughter.

Finding those three words in one bottle turned out to be harder than understanding why they worked.

I am going to skip past the next month. I read, most nights at the kitchen table after Ray went up. This is the part the twenty-nine years was for. I do not read a supplement website without checking what is underneath it.

The bitter part is real. Bitter compounds arriving in the gut trigger the release of bile. Bile does two jobs: it takes fat apart so your body can use it, and it keeps the whole lower system slippery. Both are tied to eating — specifically to eating fat.

So if you have spent months eating a fraction of what you used to eat, your body has quietly turned both of them down.

That was the sentence that stopped me. It also explained the four o'clock swelling, which I had been counting as a separate problem. It was never separate.

Three things have to be there for anything to move. Water. Fiber. Bile.

Water softens it. Fiber gives it something to hold on to. Bile makes it slide.

I had the water — eighty ounces a day. I had the fiber, a whole drawer of it.

I did not have the bile.

An eighty-six-year-old woman had said that to me in a parking lot a month earlier and I had not understood she was being literal.

Which is why everything in that drawer did what it promised and none of it ever ended. The Miralax worked. It always worked. And a few days later I needed it again. Pulling water in is not the same as putting back what went missing. The Metamucil did not even do that — bulk with nothing to move it is cement, and it made me worse more than once.

None of it was wrong. None of it was bile.

And nothing announces itself. There was no day I noticed the bile going. I just found myself doing more, getting less, and assuming it was me.

It was not only my drawer. Everything in that aisle is built for a body that is blocked. Mine was not blocked. There is no shelf for a woman who has stopped eating.

Dr. Okafor was not wrong either. She had told me the reason herself at the first visit. She just gave me the advice she gives everybody — and everybody else is eating.

So I went looking for the three words on the place card. That took me longer than the reading did. Most of what I found was one of the three on its own, or all three buried in quantities too small to matter.

I Refused to Quit My GLP-1. Here's How I Finally Solved the Constipation

I am Hannah. I've been a nurse for 38 years, and GLP-1 constipation is one of the hardest side effects I see patients struggle with. The bloating that makes them feel like a balloon. The backed-up feeling when nothing's moving through. That fear of eating because everything just... stopped. I've had patients tell me they go 7, 8, 9 days without a bowel movement. Day and night, they feel stuck.

About three years ago, it happened to me. I started Wegovy for weight management. Like my patients, I thought the constipation would be manageable. I was wrong. All those years of telling patients "just drink more water and eat fiber" — I learned firsthand how useless that advice is when you're on a GLP-1.

At first it was just going every 2-3 days instead of daily. Then came the bloating. That constant pressure in my abdomen that made me feel like I'd swallowed rocks. By the end of my shift, I could feel the backup getting worse. But the worst part? The fear. The fear of eating because I was tracking mentally how much I'd eaten that hadn't come out yet. I'd wake up on day 7 of no movement feeling genuinely scared. Would I have to go to the ER? The straining. The hours on the toilet with nothing happening. The hemorrhoids. I was exhausted, uncomfortable, and miserable no matter what I tried.

Now I was the one living with it. And let me tell you, every patient was right. It's a living hell.

My doctor suggested I could try Linzess. $600 a month for prescription-strength relief. Or maybe I should just stop the Wegovy entirely. I smiled politely. But I knew I wasn't going to do either. I'd seen too many patients quit their GLP-1 and regain all the weight — back to square one. And the ones on Linzess? The diarrhea was so severe and unpredictable they were afraid to leave home. One patient told me she had to take time off work because she couldn't be more than 30 seconds from a bathroom. For $600 a month. And for what? Most of them said it worked great at first, then their body got used to it and it stopped being effective.

I asked him if there was anything else. Anything besides a $600 prescription or quitting my medication. He looked at me like I was being difficult. Said we should "just monitor it" and "see how it goes." Three years of watching my patients struggle on these medications. Thirty-eight years in nursing. And his best advice was drink more water.

I sat in my car for ten minutes after that appointment. Just sat there. Staring at the steering wheel. I wasn't sad. I was angry. Because I've been a nurse long enough to know when a doctor is telling you he doesn't have an answer but doesn't want to say it. "Let's just monitor" is doctor for "I don't know what to do, and your problem isn't urgent enough for me to figure it out."

I wasn't about to just sit there and "monitor" while my body got worse.

So I just dealt with it. Miralax. Metamucil. Prune juice. Magnesium supplements. Bought a squatty potty. Nothing really worked, but what else was I supposed to do?

My sister found out I was spending money on supplements and natural remedies and told me I was "turning into one of those people." She said I should just listen to my doctor. Easy for her to say — she's not the one lying awake at night on day 8 wondering if she's going to end up in the ER. But this time she seemed different. More relaxed somehow.

I asked her how she was managing, and she said something I didn't expect. She told me she was actually going regularly now. She'd found some kind of herbs. The bitter ones people take for their liver. Been taking them every morning. And for the first time in a year, she was having normal bowel movements. No cramping. No laxatives. No fear.

So I pulled out my laptop and started digging. Because clearly nobody else was going to figure this out for me. Not my doctor with his "let's just monitor." Not my sister with her "listen to your doctor." Not the medical system that had nothing to offer me besides a $600 prescription that would give me different problems.

It took me about fifty minutes to find.

So you soften it (by drinking more water) and you add bulk (by taking enough fiber) and it moves. That's what my doctor was taught. That's what the whole aisle is built for. And for most people it is the right answer.

It just isn't what's happening to us. Your gut is like a tube. Things slide through it because it's greased. Your body makes the grease itself. It's called bile, and your liver sends it down when you eat. Food shows up, grease shows up.

Then you start a GLP-1, and two things go wrong at once.

First, the shot slows your whole digestive system down. Your gut, and your liver along with it. A slow liver makes less bile.

Second, you barely eat now. And bile only comes when food shows up. No food, no signal. So it makes even less.

Either one of those on its own and you'd probably cope. Both of them together and there's next to nothing left. That's why this hits so much harder than the constipation everybody else is talking about.

My gut was never full. It was dry.

That's why the fiber made things worse. Fiber in a dry tube doesn't give you a bowel movement. It gives you a bigger thing that won't move. I was eating 800 calories a day and piling in bulk on top of it.

I didn't need more stuff in there. I needed the grease back.

Bitter is what brings it back. Bitter hits your gut and your liver sends bile down, even when you haven't eaten much. That's all milk thistle, artichoke, dandelion root and beet root do.

The science actually made sense. And it made me angry — because this information isn't hard to find. It's right there. Doctors just don't look for it. They reach for the prescription pad or they say "let's monitor," and meanwhile their patients are counting days and afraid to eat dinner.

Turns out, most of these supplements are:

When it arrived, I could tell the difference immediately. The label had actual numbers on it, and 14 herbs total. Milk thistle. Artichoke. Dandelion root. Beet. Ginger. Turmeric. No psyllium, no senna, nothing that swells anywhere on the panel.

I took two with water that first morning. Again, I didn't expect much.

But by the end of that shift, I noticed something. That pressure I'd been carrying all day just wasn't there. My stomach made an actual sound — a gurgle — and I hadn't heard my own stomach in months. I went from feeling that constant pressure in my abdomen to actually feeling movement — gentle, natural movement. Like the lubrication had been switched back on for the first time in months.

That night, I had my first normal bowel movement in over a week. Actually normal — no straining. No cramping. No sitting there for 30 minutes with nothing happening. Just... normal.

When I woke up the next morning, I laid there stunned. The bloated feeling was gone. I'd slept through the night without that rock-in-my-stomach feeling for the first time in months.

By the end of the first week, I was going every single day. Every day. Not every 4-5 days like with the ones from Amazon. Every single morning like clockwork. I tracked it for three days straight because I didn't believe it. It hadn't been regular in over a year.

That bloated feeling that made me afraid to eat? Gone. The straining for hours with nothing happening? Cleared up almost completely. I could work a full shift without feeling backed up and uncomfortable.

It's been two months now. I go every single morning. Every morning. The bloating is gone. The fear is gone. Sometimes I skip a day after a really stressful shift when I'm not drinking enough water, but it's nothing. Nothing compared to what it was.

I went back to my doctor last week. Same doctor who told me to just drink water and monitor. He pulled up my chart, noted I hadn't called about the constipation in months, and actually paused. He said, "Hannah, whatever you changed, this is a significant improvement. I wasn't expecting to see this." I just smiled. I didn't tell him what I was taking. I didn't need to. I just needed to hear him say what I already knew — that I was right to keep looking.

And my sister — the one who said I was "turning into one of those people"? She called me last week. Said she could tell something was different about me. That I seemed like myself again. She asked me what I was doing. I told her about Omyo. She ordered a bottle that same night.

I saw my patient last week and thanked her. She just smiled and said she was glad it helped.

Look, for almost three years I thought I just had to live with the bloating and backed-up feeling. That this was my life now. And so was everyone who told me to stop looking for an answer. But I was wrong about giving up. And they were wrong about me.

And here's the thing — not all of these are created equal. I wasted weeks on cheap bottles that barely moved the needle. This actually-dosed formula is the only one that worked.

I've told five of my patients on GLP-1s about the one I got specifically. Every single one of them has come back and said they're finally regular again. I'm sharing this because I hope it can help someone else the way it helped me. After 38 years as a nurse, I thought I knew every option out there. Turns out, my patient knew something my doctor didn't.

I almost didn't post this, because nobody wants their name attached to a post about being backed up on Zepbound.

But I'm a nurse. Nineteen years, eleven of them prepping people for colonoscopies, and the cause turned out to be nothing like what I'd been told. I'd rather be embarrassed than watch somebody else lose five months figuring that out.

First though, I want to be clear about something, because otherwise none of the rest makes sense.

The shot worked. It worked better than anything I'd tried in forty years.

Fifty-one pounds. My A1c the best it's been in a decade. And the food noise, the thing I could never explain properly to anybody, just quiet, for the first time since I was fourteen.

I was not going to give that up.

That's the whole reason this got as bad as it did.

It wasn't that I wasn't drinking enough water. I was drinking a gallon a day and tracking it in an app.

It wasn't that I wasn't eating enough fiber.

It wasn't that I wasn't trying.

And when I finally found out what it actually was, I sat in my car in the hospital parking lot and cried.

Which is the part that still embarrasses me.

I started the shot last October. By January, three months in, this was my normal.

Nauseous most of the day. Not from the medication. From being backed up.

Cramps that woke me up at night.

So much gas and pressure I couldn't sit through a staff meeting without shifting in my chair.

Bloated to the point where I caught myself in the elevator mirror at work and thought I looked pregnant.

And the one that was hardest to describe to anybody: the constant feeling of something in there that would not move.

I messaged my doctor. I told him I hadn't gone in six days and I was worried.

He said drink more water and add some fiber.

Then he moved on to my A1c.

So I did what everybody does. I bought the list.

Metamucil first, because that's what he'd told me to do. Then psyllium husk, when the Metamucil did nothing.

Miralax, every morning, stirred into my coffee.

Magnesium citrate at night.

Stool softeners, three a day.

Prunes. Prune juice. Warm prune juice with butter in it, which is exactly as bad as it sounds.

And then eventually the thing nobody wants to admit they bought. Enemas.

Some of it worked for a week. None of it worked for a month.

By March I was planning my life around it.

I cancelled a trip to see my daughter because I couldn't face four hours in a car and then a stranger's bathroom.

I got hemorrhoids for the first time in my life. Then a fissure. I'll leave that there.

And I started doing the arithmetic that everybody on this medication eventually does.

Fifty-one pounds. The best bloodwork of my adult life. Against not being able to go to the bathroom.

I was seriously considering throwing all of it away.

That's the part I couldn't say out loud. Not to my husband. Definitely not to my doctor, because I knew exactly what he'd do. He'd cut my dose, or he'd take me off it.

So I said nothing. And I got worse.

It took a gastroenterologist I've worked beside for six years to explain it to me, and he did it in about ninety seconds standing at the coffee machine.

I'd made a joke about it. The kind of joke you make when something has stopped being funny.

He didn't laugh. He said, "What are you taking for it?"

I listed all of it.

"None of that's going to work. Every one of those is treating what's in the pipe. Nobody's looking at the pipe."

I asked him what he meant.

"Bile. Your body only puts bile out when there's food to break down. The shot means you're barely eating, so you're barely putting any out. Less food, less bile. That's the whole chain."

I said I still didn't see what that had to do with it.

"Because breaking food down isn't the only thing bile does. It's what keeps the colon slick enough for anything to move through it."

He shrugged.

"No bile, no slick. Everything dries out, goes hard, and stops. Then you put fiber on top of that. Which is a bit like unblocking a toilet by pushing more paper down it."

I went home and sat on the edge of the bed with my coat still on.

Because it explained everything. Five months of it. The prunes, the gallon of water, the fissure, the trip I cancelled. All of it aimed at the wrong end.

And it also meant there was nothing in my bathroom cabinet that was going to help me. Not one of those six things did anything about bile. They were all built to push from the bottom.

I didn't know what to do with that. So I did nothing for about three weeks, and got quietly worse.

My daughter lives four hours away.

She came down the last weekend in May, since I'd been the one to cancel.

I tried to act normal. But I couldn't sit through dinner without shifting in my seat, and she saw it.

"Mom," she said. "You're not okay."

And I told her all of it. The six days. The fissure. That I'd been thinking about stopping the medication and hadn't said it to anybody.

I hadn't cried in front of her since her father's surgery.

She didn't say much for a while.

Then she said, "I'm going to figure this out."

She's always been the one in our family who reads everything. Instruction manuals. Terms and conditions. All of it.

She called five days later. She sounded like she was walking somewhere fast.

"Mom. I think I found something."

She drove back down that weekend with a bottle in her bag.

"Before you say anything," she said. "I know exactly what you're going to say. Just read what I sent you first."

Here's what you should know about me. I am the last person alive who buys a supplement.

I have spent nineteen years watching patients bring me shopping bags of bottles they saw on Facebook.

And what's being sold to people on the shot right now is the worst of it. Half of it is the same fiber blend that was sold as a prebiotic three years ago, with GLP-1 printed on the front in a new font.

I said more or less that to her, out loud.

She said, "I know. It isn't fiber and it isn't a laxative. That's why I sent it to you."

That night I read what she'd sent.

Not marketing. Actual papers. Bile acids and how the colon moves. What happens to bile delivery when you stop eating properly.

And the whole time I kept thinking the same thing.

Why did nobody tell me this?

Nineteen years. Eleven of them handing people bowel prep instructions with a completely straight face. Why did I not know this starts with bile?

Because we treat constipation like a plumbing problem. Push harder. Add more. Drink more water.

On this medication it isn't a plumbing problem. It's a chemistry one.

The colon needs bile to stay slick. If it isn't getting any, you can pour as much fiber and water in the top as you want. You're just filling a dry pipe.

I started it on a Tuesday.

Nothing Tuesday. Nothing Wednesday.

Thursday morning I went. It wasn't dramatic. It was just easy. No straining, no bracing myself, nothing else taken alongside it.

I was still sceptical. It was one time. But it was the first bit of hope I'd had since Christmas.

Week one, I went three times.

I'd been going roughly three times in two weeks. So that number meant something to me that it wouldn't mean to anybody else.

Week two, the bloating came down enough that I noticed my waistband before I noticed the scale.

Week three, the cramping stopped. That one I hadn't expected at all, because I'd decided the cramping was just the medication and I was stuck with it.

Week five, I realised I'd stopped counting days.

For five months I'd had a number in my head at all times. What day I was on. I didn't decide to stop tracking it. I just noticed one morning that I didn't know it anymore.

Last month I drove the four hours to my daughter's house. I didn't plan anything around it. I just went.

I had my follow-up in July.

Same doctor. The one who told me to drink more water.

He asked how I was getting on with everything, and I told him the truth for the first time in eight months. That I'd come within about two weeks of quitting his medication, and that I hadn't told him because I was afraid he'd take it off me.

He was quiet for a second.

Then he asked what I'd changed.

I told him.

He wrote the name down on the back of a card.

And then he said, "I wish I'd known to tell you that eight months ago."

Me too.

Because if I'd known in January I'd have kept the trip. I wouldn't have the fissure. I wouldn't have spent five months lying to my own doctor.

That's why I'm putting this on the internet with my name on it.

If any of this is your life right now.

You're straining in there and nothing comes out.

You're counting days. You know exactly what day you're on.

You're backed up to the point where you're nauseous from it.

You've bought the entire list and nothing holds for more than a week.

And you've started asking yourself whether it's worth it.

Then read this next part, because I'd like to save you the five months.

Before you go looking for something like this, let me save you the money I wasted first.

Almost everything sold to people on the shot is fiber. Turn the bottle over and read it. If the first thing on there is psyllium, or inulin, or a prebiotic blend, that's the thing that made me worse.

The rest of it is laxatives with a nicer label. Dulcolax, senna, Smooth Move. Those work the first time. Then they work less. Then you need more.

I prepped colonoscopy patients for eleven years. I've seen on a screen what taking one of those every day does to a colon. I wouldn't do it, and I wouldn't let my mother do it.

The one my daughter found is called Omyo.

It does two things, and the first one is the part nothing else on that shelf touches. Milk thistle, dandelion and beetroot. That's the bile group.

Bile comes back, the pipe goes slick again, and things move the way they're meant to. That's the whole sequence, and it starts at the top, which is the end I'd been ignoring for five months.

Fiber doesn't do that. Magnesium doesn't do that. A probiotic doesn't do that. It's the reason all six things in my cabinet failed.

Then ginger and artichoke, for the squeeze. Your gut moves everything along by squeezing, wave after wave, and on this medication that slows right down with the rest of you. Because slick on its own isn't enough. Something still has to push.

No senna. Nothing that forces anything. Nothing that wants a bigger dose next month.

Two capsules, before bed. That's the whole thing.

Fourteen ingredients, and I read every one of them, because that's what I do. There wasn't one I had to look up, and there wasn't one I'd have flagged for a patient. It's plants. That's the whole list.

What I can tell you is that it's the only thing in five months that changed anything.

I ordered three the next time round.

Two for me, because I'd already worked out what happens if I run out and I wasn't willing to find out again. And one for a friend from church who's been on the shot since last spring.

She rang me about three weeks later, and she was crying.

She said, "I didn't realise how bad I'd been feeling until I stopped feeling like that."

There are six of us at my hospital on it now. All of us on the shot. Every single one of us had the same six bottles sitting in the bathroom cabinet.

One of the nurses on my floor didn't order it when I told her about it. She meant to. You know how that goes.

She stopped the medication in April instead. She'd lost thirty pounds and her blood pressure was normal for the first time in years, and she gave it up because she couldn't take one more week of this.

She's put nineteen of it back on.

She said to me last month, "I wish I'd just ordered it when you told me."

That's the one I think about. Not the bad days. The people who did everything right, finally got the thing they'd been chasing for years, and handed it back over something that had a fix nobody bothered to tell them about.

So that's it. That's all I wanted to say.

You're not failing at this. You were given the wrong instructions. Water and fiber is the right advice for ordinary constipation, and this isn't ordinary constipation.

And you shouldn't have to choose between the medication that's finally working and being able to live in your own body.

If you try it and it does nothing, they give you your money back. That's the only reason I was willing to spend anything at all on it, after the year I'd had.

I spent five months treating the bottom of a pipe that was dry at the top.

You don't have to.

EDIT, four days later. I did not expect any of this. My messages are a mess and I'm sorry to everybody I haven't got back to yet.

Most of you are asking the same two things, so I'll just put them here.

6 months on the shot. 36 pounds down. 6 days since I'd gone.

And at my daughter's wedding, an 86-year-old Greek woman I had never met asked me the one question nobody else had thought to ask.

I am Hannah. I am fifty-four. I have two daughters. In April the younger one, Kate, married a Greek boy named Nikos, down in Florida. I spent twenty-nine years in medical records at a hospital in central Ohio. Not a nurse. I filed charts, coded charts and read charts. That matters later, because it is the only reason I checked any of this.

I had never been to a Greek wedding. I packed a box of Miralax for it.

Here is what the six months actually looked like.

I started last October. By the wedding I was down thirty-six pounds and my blood pressure was 118 over 74, a number I had not seen on myself since I was thirty-five. The first two months I was happier than I had been in ten years. I would make the same decision again tomorrow.

Then somewhere in the second month, I stopped going.

Not slowed down. Stopped.

Three days. Then five. In January I went seven, and by the seventh day there was an ache low on the left side, and I spent an afternoon in the bathroom with the door locked, pressing on my own stomach and reading about what a blockage feels like.

The part I could not explain to my husband Ray was that I was not hungry at all and I was swollen all the time. I was eating maybe eight hundred calories a day and I looked six months pregnant by four in the afternoon.

Then the rest of it arrived. Tired in a way that walking did not fix. Not sleepy. Heavy. The scale sat at 189 for three weeks and I could not tell you whether the medicine had quit on me or whether I was carrying a week of it around. Ray asked if I was all right. I said I was fine.

I was not fine, and I could not have told him which part of it was making me not fine.

And I had a drawer.

If you have a drawer like this you already know where this is going.

Miralax. A tub of it, and a second one behind it. Metamucil, orange, half gone, because I could not get the last swallow down without gagging. Stool softeners, two brands. Fiber gummies. Prune juice. Chia seeds. A bag of ground flax that went rancid in the pantry.

And a note on my phone where I tracked the days.

I went to my doctor about it twice. Dr. Okafor is a good doctor and I want to be fair to her. Bloodwork normal. Nothing on the exam.

Both times she told me the same thing, honestly: "Hannah, this is the most common thing I deal with on these medications. You are eating a fraction of what you used to eat. Less going in means less coming out."

Hold on to that sentence. She was right, and it still cost me five more months.

Then she told me to drink more water. Eat more fiber. Walk. Keep the Miralax going.

I walked out of that office both times feeling believed and completely alone.

Because I was already drinking eighty ounces a day. I was already walking. And I was eating so little that "more fiber" did not connect to anything real. More fiber on top of what? I was not eating enough for fiber to hold on to.

So I did what I think most women do. I pushed harder. A stronger thing whenever the softer thing stopped working.

In February they moved me up a dose. Nobody told me what that would do to the other thing. And the number on my phone stopped coming back down.

Two weeks before the wedding, I sat in my car in a grocery store parking lot and did arithmetic.

I worked out how many pounds I would put back on if I stopped the shot. How long it would take. What I would say to Kate and to Ray.

I sat there for eleven minutes seriously considering giving back the best six months my body has had in twenty years, because I could not go to the bathroom.

I know I am not the only woman who has done that math in a parked car. I also know women who finished the math and stopped. Not one of them stopped because the shot was not working. They stopped because of this.

I did not stop. I went to the wedding — where a stranger asked me for the number I had never said out loud.

If you have never sat through a Greek reception, it is food, and it does not stop coming. Refusing it is not a diet choice in that room. It is close to an insult.

And I could not eat. I moved lamb around a plate for two hours with my hand flat on my stomach under the tablecloth, because the pressure was making it hard to sit up straight.

Nikos's grandmother was seated to my left. Her name was Eleni. Eighty-six, small, in black, white hair pinned back. She ate slowly and not much. She got up twice to cross the room, both times without pushing off the table.

About two hours in she turned to me and said: "Hannah. May I ask you something rude?"

I said of course.

She said: "You are not eating. And you are still full. How many days?"

I froze.

I had not told anybody that number. Not Ray. Not Kate. Not my sister. It was a note on my phone and I had never once said it out loud to another human being.

I said: "What do you mean?"

She said: "You have had your hand on your stomach since you sat down. You have moved the same piece of lamb four times. You have not eaten, and you are not hungry, and you are still swollen. I know that. How many days?"

I sat at my own daughter's wedding and said: "Six."

She nodded. She asked if I was eating so little because I was sick. I said no — I was on one of the shots, for the weight.

I said that part easily. Everybody knows somebody on one now. That was not the hard thing to say at that table. The hard thing to say was "six."

She said: "I do not know anything about your shot. But I know about not eating."

Then she turned back to her plate and finished eating.

Ray had asked me if I was all right. More than once. That was the question he had. He did not have the other one — and he had been looking at me every day for twenty-six years, which turns out to be the worst way to notice that something has changed.

Eleni had never seen me before in her life. She had two hours and clear eyes.

Ten minutes later she set her fork down and asked me to walk outside with her.

She took me out the side door to a concrete yard where they park the vans. There was a card table against the fence, in the shade, with newspaper on it, and on the newspaper were bunches of something long-stemmed and dark and wild-looking, half wilted from the sun.

"Do you know these?"

I said no.

"Horta. Wild greens. Dandelion. Chicory. Artichoke. We boil them with lemon. They are bitter. Americans do not like them."

She picked up a stem and held it out to me. Then she asked: "Do you know that we fast?"

I said I knew a little. Lent, I assumed.

"Not only Lent. Wednesday. Friday. Forty days before Easter. Forty before Christmas. Half of every year for eighty years I have eaten almost nothing. My mother the same. Her mother the same. We have known for a very long time what happens to a woman's body when the food stops."

I asked what happens.

"Everything stops. Not just the eating. Everything."

And then she said the thing I have thought about nearly every day since.

"You keep trying to push. Nobody has asked you what stopped."

I did not have an answer.

She meant that literally. I did not hear it that way for another month.

She sat down on a folding chair and told me about her husband. Kostas died in 2011, and she stopped eating — not on purpose, the way people stop eating when the person they cooked for is gone. Coffee and bread for most of a year.

By spring she had exactly what I had. Nothing moving. Swollen all the time. Not hungry at all.

Her own doctor told her to drink more water.

Her aunt, ninety-one, drove over, looked in her kitchen, and told her what the old women there all know.

Eleni told it to me standing in that lot in her black dress with a bunch of dandelion greens in her hand.

"When you eat, your liver sends down the bitter water. That is what takes your food apart. That is what makes everything slide."

"When you stop eating, the liver goes to sleep. Nothing comes down. So the food sits. It goes heavy. It goes sour. And nothing moves."

"You are not blocked. You are dry."

I asked what you do about it.

"You eat something bitter. The gut tells the liver. The liver does not know whether food is coming. It only knows bitter. That is why we eat these. Not because it is healthy. Because it is bitter."

I asked what happened to her after she started again. She said seven weeks, maybe eight. And then she stopped counting the days, and has not worried about it since.

I spent twenty-nine years reading charts. I am not a person who takes medical advice from a folding chair in a parking lot.

But I could not stop thinking about the fact that an eighty-six-year-old woman had watched me for two hours and known the number.

I asked her whether she really expected me to start boiling weeds. She laughed at me — the first time she laughed all night — and said: "They probably sell the bitter part in a bottle now. Ask at a pharmacy."

Then she took a place card off the nearest table, turned it over, and wrote three words on the back in shaky capitals.

Dandelion. Chicory. Artichoke.

She handed it to me and said: "These three. This is what your body is asking for. Ask your doctor before you take anything. If she says no, do not take it. But ask her."

I put the place card in my purse and went back inside and danced with my daughter.

Finding those three words in one bottle turned out to be harder than understanding why they worked.

I am going to skip past the next month. I read, most nights at the kitchen table after Ray went up. This is the part the twenty-nine years was for. I do not read a supplement website without checking what is underneath it.

The bitter part is real. Bitter compounds arriving in the gut trigger the release of bile. Bile does two jobs: it takes fat apart so your body can use it, and it keeps the whole lower system slippery. Both are tied to eating — specifically to eating fat.

So if you have spent months eating a fraction of what you used to eat, your body has quietly turned both of them down.

That was the sentence that stopped me. It also explained the four o'clock swelling, which I had been counting as a separate problem. It was never separate.

Three things have to be there for anything to move. Water. Fiber. Bile.

Water softens it. Fiber gives it something to hold on to. Bile makes it slide.

I had the water — eighty ounces a day. I had the fiber, a whole drawer of it.

I did not have the bile.

An eighty-six-year-old woman had said that to me in a parking lot a month earlier and I had not understood she was being literal.

Which is why everything in that drawer did what it promised and none of it ever ended. The Miralax worked. It always worked. And a few days later I needed it again. Pulling water in is not the same as putting back what went missing. The Metamucil did not even do that — bulk with nothing to move it is cement, and it made me worse more than once.

None of it was wrong. None of it was bile.

And nothing announces itself. There was no day I noticed the bile going. I just found myself doing more, getting less, and assuming it was me.

It was not only my drawer. Everything in that aisle is built for a body that is blocked. Mine was not blocked. There is no shelf for a woman who has stopped eating.

Dr. Okafor was not wrong either. She had told me the reason herself at the first visit. She just gave me the advice she gives everybody — and everybody else is eating.

So I went looking for the three words on the place card. That took me longer than the reading did. Most of what I found was one of the three on its own, or all three buried in quantities too small to matter.

The one I kept coming back to is called Omyo.

I looked at what is in it, because that is the part I know how to read. Milk thistle. Beet root. Burdock. Yellow dock. Barberry. Ginger. Turmeric. All bitter. All the same idea.

And in with them: dandelion root, chicory root, artichoke leaf. All three words on the back of that place card, in one bottle, at real dosages.

It was not built for constipation in general. It was built for people on the shot who are eating a fraction of what they used to. That is the entire reason the bitter herbs are in it and the fiber is not.

And in all that time looking for help, I had never once come across it.

I did what Eleni told me to do first. I called Dr. Okafor's office on a Tuesday and told the nurse the whole ridiculous story — the wedding, the grandmother, the wild greens.

She called back Thursday. "Dr. Okafor says bitter herbs for digestion is not a new idea and it is not a concerning one. Go ahead. Add it, don't stop anything you were already doing, and tell her at your next visit how it went."

I ordered a bottle that night and started the following Monday. Two capsules with a glass of water in the morning. I did not change one other thing.

Here is what happened, in the order it happened — including the part I wish somebody had warned me about.

For the first two weeks, nothing. I would have wanted to know that.

Around week three, on a Thursday, I was standing at the counter making Ray's coffee and realised my waistband was not sitting on top of anything. I had gotten so used to the four o'clock swelling that its absence did not feel like relief. It felt like nothing. It took me a second to work out what was different.

Somewhere after that I stopped checking the note on my phone every morning.

I went back and looked at it later. It had been six and five and six right up until I started.

It was two and three and two.

I had not registered it happening.

I want to be careful here, because this is where these letters usually get carried away. I am not a doctor. I filed the charts. I do not know for certain that the Omyo is what changed it — nobody can know that from one person and a few months. I know what I was doing before, what I added, that I changed nothing else, and when it happened.

I am also not going to tell you it fixed everything. I still get tired. I am still fifty-four.

If you have spent months eating a fraction of what you used to eat, and things have gone quiet, and you have been told to drink more water and eat more fiber by somebody who was being perfectly kind and perfectly unhelpful — and you have a drawer —

Nobody quits over the number on the scale. They quit over this. They quit in a parking lot, over something they will not say out loud.

That is the whole story.

P.S. If you decide to try it: two capsules with a glass of water in the morning, and do not change anything else. Give it a few weeks. Some women notice something in the first week or two. I did not — mine was week three. A liver that has been asleep for six months does not wake up on a Tuesday. And do not go looking for the three plants separately the way I did first. I wasted two weeks on that.

P.P.S. We drove back down in October and Kate met us there. Eleni was on the porch when we pulled up, with a bag of greens washed and waiting for us to take home. She held me out at arm's length, looked at my face, and said: "Better." She is eighty-seven now. She still gets out of the chair without pushing off the table. Before we left she asked whether I had told anyone. I said three women in my walking group. She said: "Good. Tell them properly. Not on the sidewalk."

So here it is, properly.
